title: Sort List
directAnswer: Sort a linked list in O(n log n) time by running merge sort directly on the nodes. Split the list into two halves using the fast/slow pointer trick, recursively sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves with a dummy-node splice. Merge sort is the right choice (not quicksort or heapsort) because it needs only sequential access and merges linked lists in O(1) extra space per merge — exactly what a singly linked list offers. The recursion stack costs O(log n); for true O(1) space, switch to bottom-up merge sort.

remember.pattern: Merge sort on a linked list — split by fast/slow, sort halves, merge
remember.formula:
sort(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None: return head
    mid = split(head)            # fast/slow, CUT before mid
    left  = sort(head)
    right = sort(mid)
    return merge(left, right)     # dummy + tail splice
rules: Use **merge sort**, not quicksort — linked lists give sequential access and O(1) merges, but no cheap random pivot access.
Find the middle with **fast/slow pointers**, then **sever the link** before the second half (`prev.next = null`) or the recursion never terminates.
Base case is `head == null || head.next == null` — a list of 0 or 1 nodes is already sorted.
Merge with a **dummy head + tail pointer** so the first splice needs no special case; return `dummy.next`.
The recursive top-down version is O(log n) stack space. Mention **bottom-up** merge sort for the true O(1)-space answer interviewers love.

remember.takeaway: Merge sort is THE sort for linked lists: it only walks forward, merges in O(1) space, and is stable. Master split-via-fast/slow and dummy-node merge here and you've built the two reusable primitives behind Merge Two Sorted Lists, Merge k Sorted Lists, and the merge step of any divide-and-conquer.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know merge sort is the natural O(n log n) sort for linked lists — and can implement the two sub-routines (split by fast/slow, merge by dummy node) cleanly without losing or cycling nodes.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting to cut the list at the midpoint (so the two halves still share nodes and recursion never bottoms out), or reaching for quicksort and getting tangled in pivot partitioning on a singly linked list.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Implement top-down cleanly, then say: 'This is O(log n) stack space; the bottom-up iterative version gets us to O(1) space.' Naming that upgrade signals you understand WHY merge sort wins on lists.

problemStatement:
Given the `head` of a linked list, return *the list after sorting it in **ascending order***.

The follow-up: can you sort the list in `O(n log n)` time and `O(1)` memory (i.e. constant space)?
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [0, 5 × 10⁴]
understanding: We must reorder the existing nodes of a singly linked list so their values are non-decreasing. Because a linked list has no random access, the array tricks (quickselect pivots, index arithmetic) don't apply cleanly — we sort by repeatedly splitting the list in half and merging sorted halves back together. The list may be empty or a single node, both of which are trivially sorted.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I sort in place by rewiring nodes, or is allocating an array of values acceptable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The follow-up explicitly asks for O(1) memory, so the intended answer rewires nodes. I'll present the pointer-based merge sort; dumping to an array is the easy fallback worth mentioning.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is it a singly or doubly linked list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Singly linked (standard ListNode with only `next`). That's why merge sort beats quicksort here — we only ever traverse forward.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can values be negative or duplicated?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes to both (-10⁵ to 10⁵, duplicates allowed). Merge sort is stable, so equal values keep their relative order, and negatives need no special handling.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the sort need to be stable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not required by the prompt, but merge sort gives stability for free using `<=` in the merge comparison — worth stating as a bonus.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Dump to Array, Sort, Rebuild
approaches.whenToMention: State it first as the simple baseline: 'If O(n) extra space is fine, I can copy values out, sort, and write them back.' Then pivot to merge sort for the O(1)-space follow-up.
hints: A linked list is hard to sort directly, but an array is trivial — the library sort is O(n log n). Can you move the data into a structure you already know how to sort?
Walk the list once collecting every value into an array, sort the array, then walk the list a second time overwriting each node's value in sorted order.
You never touch the `next` pointers — the node structure stays identical, only the `val` fields are rewritten. That's why it's so simple, and also why it costs O(n) extra space.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Collecting values is O(n), sorting the array is O(n log n), rewriting is O(n) → O(n log n) total. The array of n values is O(n) extra space, which violates the follow-up's O(1) requirement.
approaches.explanation:
This approach sidesteps the hard part of the problem entirely. The difficulty in sorting a linked list comes from the lack of random access — but an array *has* random access and a battle-tested O(n log n) library sort. So we borrow the array: copy every node's value into a list, sort that list, then walk the original nodes a second time and overwrite each `val` with the next sorted value.

**Why this is worth saying out loud.** Interviewers want to see you reduce an unfamiliar problem to a familiar one. 'Sort a linked list' becomes 'sort an array' the moment you decouple the *values* from the *node structure*. It's correct, it's fast, and it takes thirty seconds to write — a perfectly good answer if the constraints don't forbid extra space.

**Why it doesn't satisfy the follow-up.** The whole point of LeetCode 148's follow-up is the phrase *O(1) memory*. The auxiliary array holds all n values, so this is O(n) space. It also feels like cheating — you're not really sorting the list, you're sorting an array and copying answers back. The interviewer will almost always respond with 'nice, now do it without the extra array', which is your cue to bring out merge sort.

**The subtle correctness point.** Because we only overwrite `val` and never re-link nodes, the list's shape is preserved and there's zero risk of creating a cycle or dropping a node. That safety is the upside of trading space for simplicity — but it's exactly that extra array we're asked to eliminate.
approaches.insight: Reducing 'sort a linked list' to 'sort an array' is the canonical trick of mapping a hard structure onto an easy one. Always mention it — it proves you can simplify — but be ready for the interviewer to immediately raise the space bar, which forces the real answer.

dryRun.intro: Copy values out, sort the array, write them back into the same nodes in order.

code.python:
def sortList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    vals = []
    cur = head
    while cur:
        vals.append(cur.val)
        cur = cur.next
    vals.sort()
    cur = head
    for v in vals:
        cur.val = v
        cur = cur.next
    return head

approaches.name: Top-Down Merge Sort (Optimal, O(log n) stack)
approaches.whenToMention: The expected answer. Lead with 'merge sort is the natural fit for linked lists' and structure it as the three primitives: split, recurse, merge.
hints: Merge sort works by sorting two halves and merging them. You already know how to merge two sorted lists in O(1) space — so the only new piece is splitting a list into two halves.

Split with the fast/slow pointer trick: advance `fast` two steps and `slow` one step; when `fast` reaches the end, `slow` is at the middle. Keep a `prev` so you can cut the list with `prev.next = null`.
Recurse on each half, base-casing when the list has 0 or 1 nodes, then merge the two sorted results with a dummy-head splice and return `dummy.next`.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each recursion level processes all n nodes across its merges (n total work per level), and the list halves each level, so there are log n levels → O(n log n) time. The recursion goes log n deep, so the call stack is O(log n) space; no auxiliary arrays are allocated, only pointers rewired.
approaches.explanation:
Merge sort is the textbook divide-and-conquer sort, and a linked list is the structure it was practically designed for. The algorithm is three steps: **divide** the list into two halves, **conquer** by recursively sorting each half, and **combine** by merging the two sorted halves into one. The base case is a list of zero or one node, which is already sorted, so recursion bottoms out there.

**Why merge sort and not quicksort or heapsort.** A singly linked list only supports sequential, forward access — there's no O(1) 'jump to index k'. Quicksort's partition step wants to swap elements around a pivot, which is painful without random access and degrades to O(n²) on adversarial input. Heapsort needs an array-backed heap. Merge sort, by contrast, only ever walks forward and its merge step splices two sorted lists in **O(1) extra space** by rewiring `next` pointers. The structure's one weakness (no random access) simply doesn't matter to merge sort, and its one strength (cheap splicing) is exactly what merge exploits.

**The split sub-routine, and why `prev` matters.** To divide, we find the midpoint with the fast/slow pointer trick: `fast` moves two nodes per step, `slow` moves one, so when `fast` falls off the end, `slow` sits at the middle. The critical detail is that finding the middle isn't enough — we must **sever** the list into two independent lists. We track the node *before* `slow` (call it `prev`) and set `prev.next = null`. Skip this cut and the 'two halves' still share nodes; the recursion on the second half walks right back into the first half, never shrinks the input, and you get infinite recursion or a stack overflow. The cut is what makes the subproblems strictly smaller.

**The merge sub-routine, reused wholesale.** Combining is exactly *Merge Two Sorted Lists*: a dummy head, a tail pointer, and a loop attaching the smaller current node until one list empties, then splicing the remainder in one link. Using a dummy node means the first attachment needs no special case, and returning `dummy.next` hands back the real head. Using `<=` in the comparison keeps equal values in their original order, making the whole sort stable.

**Putting the cost together.** Every level of the recursion does O(n) total work (the merges at that level collectively touch all n nodes), and because each split halves the list, the depth is log n levels — hence O(n log n) time, the optimal comparison-sort bound. The only non-constant space is the recursion stack at depth log n, so this is O(log n) space — close to, but not quite, the follow-up's O(1) target, which the bottom-up variant achieves.
approaches.insight: Merge sort on a list is just two reusable primitives glued together: split-by-fast/slow and merge-by-dummy-node. If you can write Middle of the Linked List and Merge Two Sorted Lists, you can write this — the recursion is the trivial part. Recognizing problems as compositions of primitives you already own is how you stay calm under interview pressure.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up Merge Sort (True O(1) Space)
approaches.whenToMention: Bring this up for the O(1)-memory follow-up: 'top-down is O(log n) stack; going iterative bottom-up removes the recursion and gets us to constant space.'
hints: The recursion stack is the only thing keeping top-down from O(1) space. Can you produce the same merges iteratively, smallest sublists first?
Merge sublists of size 1 into runs of size 2, then merge size-2 runs into size-4, doubling the run length each outer pass until it exceeds n.
For each pass, walk the list cutting off two consecutive runs of the current size, merge them, and stitch the result onto a running tail using a dummy head.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are log n doubling passes; each pass walks and merges all n nodes in O(n) → O(n log n) time. Everything is done with a fixed set of pointers and an explicit split/merge — no recursion, no arrays — so space is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Bottom-up merge sort produces exactly the same merges as top-down but schedules them iteratively, eliminating the recursion stack and hitting the follow-up's O(1) space target. Instead of splitting top-down, we build the sorted result up from the smallest pieces: first treat each node as a sorted run of length 1, merge adjacent runs into runs of length 2, then merge those into runs of length 4, and so on, doubling the run length each outer pass until it covers the whole list.

**Why it's O(1) space.** There is no recursion, so there is no call stack growing with n, and we allocate no auxiliary array. The algorithm uses a fixed handful of pointers — a dummy head, a tail, and cursors to carve out the two runs being merged — regardless of list size. That's the entire reason this variant exists: it's the only version that truly answers 'O(1) memory'.

**The machinery: split off a run, merge, repeat.** Each outer pass fixes a `size`. We sweep the list left to right: detach a run of `size` nodes (call it `left`), then detach the next `size` nodes (`right`), merge them with the same dummy-node merge from before, and append the merged run to a `tail` that accumulates the fully-processed prefix. We keep a helper that walks `size−1` steps and cuts the link to return the head of what remains. We repeat until the whole list is consumed for this pass, then double `size`.

**Why it produces a sorted list.** After the pass with `size = 1`, every adjacent pair is internally sorted (runs of length ≤ 2). After `size = 2`, every group of four is sorted, and so on. Each pass maintains the invariant that the list is a sequence of sorted runs of length `size` (the last run may be shorter), and merging adjacent runs doubles their length while keeping them sorted. Once `size >= n`, the entire list is one sorted run and we stop.

**The honest trade-off.** Bottom-up is fiddlier to code correctly under pressure — the split-and-stitch bookkeeping is where bugs hide — so in an interview it's often best to write the clean top-down version first, get it correct, then describe (or implement if asked) the bottom-up upgrade. Stating that you know the O(1) version exists and why it works frequently earns the credit even without flawless on-the-spot code.
approaches.insight: Top-down vs bottom-up is the recursion-vs-iteration duality applied to divide-and-conquer: same total work, same merges, but bottom-up trades the implicit call stack for explicit iteration and wins O(log n) → O(1) space. This 'remove the recursion to save stack space' move recurs in tree traversals (Morris traversal) and DP (rolling arrays).

dryRun.intro: Double the run size each pass: 1 → 2 → 4. n = 4, so two passes suffice.

code.python:
def sortList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head

    n = 0
    cur = head
    while cur:
        n += 1
        cur = cur.next

    dummy = ListNode(0)
    dummy.next = head

    size = 1
    while size < n:
        prev, cur = dummy, dummy.next
        while cur:
            left = cur
            right = self._split(left, size)
            cur = self._split(right, size)      # start of next block
            prev = self._merge_into(prev, left, right)
        size *= 2
    return dummy.next

def _split(self, head: Optional[ListNode], size: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    i = 1
    while head and i < size:
        head = head.next
        i += 1
    if head is None:
        return None
    rest = head.next
    head.next = None
    return rest

def _merge_into(self, prev: ListNode, a: Optional[ListNode], b: Optional[ListNode]) -> ListNode:
    tail = prev
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next = a
            a = a.next
        else:
            tail.next = b
            b = b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a if a else b
    while tail.next:
        tail = tail.next
    return tail

java.explanation: Outer pass doubles the run length: 1, 2, 4, ... until it covers the list.
Cut off the first run; right heads the second run.
Cut off the second run; cur heads the next block to process this pass.
Merge the two runs onto the growing tail and advance prev to the new tail.
Walk to the true end so the next merge appends after all merged nodes.

python.explanation: Doubling passes; stops once one run spans the whole list.
Detach the first run of length size; right starts the second run.
Detach the second run; cur is where the next block begins.
Merge and stitch onto the accumulating tail.
Advance to the actual tail so subsequent blocks attach correctly.

pitfalls: Forgetting to walk tail to its real end after merge — the next block gets attached in the wrong place.
Off-by-one in split (using i < size vs i <= size) — cuts runs of the wrong length.

Reaching for this version first under time pressure — write top-down, then upgrade.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to sever the list at the midpoint (prev.next = null), causing infinite recursion.
Choosing quicksort and struggling with pivot partitioning on a singly linked list.
Claiming the dump-to-array solution is O(1) space — the array is O(n).
Returning the dummy node instead of dummy.next from the merge helper.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not cutting the list at the midpoint
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Finding `slow` as the middle isn't enough. If you don't set `prev.next = null`, the 'first half' still links into the second half, so sortList(head) walks the entire list every time, the input never shrinks, and you get infinite recursion / stack overflow.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning the dummy sentinel instead of dummy.next
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The dummy node has value 0 (or whatever you initialized) and is only a scaffold to avoid first-node special cases. Returning it prepends a bogus node to your sorted list.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
dummy = ListNode(0)
tail = dummy
# ... merge loop ...
return dummy   # includes the fake 0 node
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
dummy = ListNode(0)
tail = dummy
# ... merge loop ...
return dummy.next   # the real head of the merged list

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Calling the dump-to-array version O(1) space
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The follow-up demands O(1) memory. An auxiliary list/array holding all n values is O(n) space — be precise about this when you present the baseline, and switch to merge sort for the real answer.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
vals = [c.val for c in iterate(head)]  # O(n) extra space
vals.sort()
# ... write back ...  -> NOT O(1) memory
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# Pointer-based merge sort rewires existing nodes:
# top-down = O(log n) stack, bottom-up = O(1) space.

patternNote: Divide-and-conquer merge sort on a linked list. Recognize it whenever you must sort a list in O(n log n) with only sequential access — merge sort is the answer because its merge step is O(1) space and it never needs random access. It composes the fast/slow split (Middle of the Linked List) with the dummy-node merge (Merge Two Sorted Lists), the same merge that scales up to Merge k Sorted Lists.
